title: Why Transition Metals Have High Melting Points
subject: Chemistry
objective: In transition metals the (n−1)d electrons join the ns electrons in metallic bonding, so the bonds are strong and the metals are hard with high melting points. Across the 3d series melting points peak near the middle (Mn is an exception) and fall to zinc (d¹⁰).

fill.q: In transition metals, (n−1)d electrons take part in ____ bonding along with ns electrons.
In the 3d series, melting points are highest near the ____ of the series.
The anomalously low melting point in the middle of the 3d series is shown by ____.
The transition-group metal that is liquid at room temperature is ____.

tf.q: Zinc has the lowest melting point in the 3d series.
More electrons in metallic bonding give weaker bonds.
tf.explain: More bonding electrons give stronger bonds.

tf.q: Tungsten is used in bulb filaments because of its very high melting point.

ar.a: Zinc has a low melting point.
ar.r: Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell with no unpaired d electrons for bonding.

ar.a: Chromium has a high melting point.
ar.explain: Both true; R does not explain A: many unpaired d electrons bond.

short.q: Why do melting points rise to a maximum near the middle of the 3d series and then fall?
short.solution: The number of unpaired d electrons available for metallic bonding grows up to about d⁵, then electrons pair up and fewer take part.
